newsitem.title: UK: Sinn Fein in N.Irish talk arena as Unionist exits.
newsitem.headline: Sinn Fein in N.Irish talk arena as Unionist exits.

text.p: A convicted IRA bomber opened Sinn Fein's office at Belfast peace talks on Monday. A diehard pro-British Protestant walked out of the talks minutes later.

The two actions underlined the gulf that Britain and Ireland are trying to bridge in their search for a settlement to the Northern Ireland conflict between pro-British unionists and Catholic Irish nationalists that has claimed around 3,200 lives since 1969.

Sinn Fein's Gerry Kelly opened the office at the Belfast peace talks from which his party was barred for 13 months until its Irish Republican Army guerrilla allies declared a new ceasefire at the weekend.
Twenty-two hours after the IRA nded hostilities, Kelly and party aide Siobhan O'Hanlon became the first Sinn Fein delegates to enter the venue for 13-month-old Anglo-Irish peace talks.

Previously Sinn Fein politicians found the wire mesh gates bolted against them but Sunday's "complete cessation of military operations" by the IRA was the key that Britain said would open the door to the Stormont buildings in a parkland complex that once housed a Northern Ireland legislature.
But minutes after the Sinn Fein delegates arrived at the drab government offices where Britain co-hosts the multi-party talks with Ireland, one of the three Protestant unionist parties stormed out.
Robert McCartney, leader of the tiny United Kingdom Unionist Party and a scourge of republican guerrilla groups, accused the British and Irish governments of "terrorist appeasement".
A skilled lawyer and outspoken pro-British member of parliament, McCartney held court for some 15 minutes outside the complex delivering his verdict on British and Irish politicking.
He voiced fury over what unionists regard as a weak-kneed approach by Britain and Ireland to achieving disarmament by the IRA and Protestant loyalist militias.

"The representatives of political terror have been strengthened at the expense of democratic politicians and the confidence of the pro-Union people that the government will protect their constitutional rights has never ever been lower," McCartney said in a statement.
He said he would be back only to cast a vote against "arms decommissioning" proposals by Britain and Ireland due to be taken at a crunch meeting of the multi-party talks on Wednesday.
The proposals say that parties will no longer be expected to disarm as a condition for taking part in the talks but during them, a concession unionists fear will mean never.

McCartney's walkout eclipsed a moment of deep symbolism for Sinn Fein. Its leaders, Gerry Adams and Martin McGuinness, twice tried to get into Stormont over the past year but had the gates locked in front of them.
Sinn Fein is allowed to use its office facilities but is still barred from a conference seat until September 15 while Britain assesses whether the IRA truce is genuine.

Living up to the "quiet man" nickname the British gave him because of his silence during previous Sinn Fein talks with government officials, Kelly spoke for a minute to reporters saying he and O'Hanlon were there for "preliminary meetings".

Kelly was jailed for the IRA bombing of London's Old Bailey court complex in 1972. He escaped from a British jail in the 1980s and was extradited from the Netherlands. He has been on the party's negotiating team since returning to Belfast.

Inside the east Belfast office complex Kelly, who spent a total of 15 years in jail and twice escaped from prison, and O'Hanlon were being shown to their quarters and finding their way along the corridors of power.
Later they were joined by Sinn Fein chairman Mitchel McLaughlin who said that the republican objective of a United Ireland state would be on the agenda for the September 15 talks.
He was confident that unionists would not turn their back on the process. "I believe those who walk out of talks will return. The door should be left open so that that can happen," he said.
